meta.title: In Vivo CD4+ T Cell Differentiation and Function: Revisiting the Th1/Th2 Paradigm
affiliations: Department of Immunology, University of Washington School of Medicine, Seattle, Washington 98109, USA; email: mikelr@uw.edumpepper@uw.edu

abstractHtml:
The discovery of CD4+ T cell subset–defining master transcription factors and framing of the Th1/Th2 paradigm ignited the CD4+ T cell field. Advances in in vivo experimental systems, however, have revealed that more complex lineage-defining transcriptional networks direct CD4+ T cell differentiation in the lymphoid organs and tissues. This review focuses on the layers of fate decisions that inform CD4+ T cell differentiation in vivo. Cytokine production by antigen-presenting cells and other innate cells influences the CD4+ T cell effector program [e.g., T helper type 1 (Th1), Th2, Th17]. Signals downstream of the T cell receptor influence whether individual clones bearing hallmarks of this effector program become T follicular helper cells, supporting development of B cells expressing specific antibody isotypes, or T effector cells, which activate microbicidal innate cells in tissues. These bifurcated, parallel axes allow CD4+ T cells to augment their particular effector program and prevent disease.

Keyword(s): CD4+ subset, CD4+ T cell differentiation, memory T cell, T effector cell, T follicular helper cell, transcription factor

blocks.html: CD4<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> T cells are important activators of both the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system. They are critical protectors from infectious diseases but can also propagate allergy and autoimmunity. Understanding how to drive specific CD4<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> subsets by vaccination or alter their function to suppress pathology is therefore a critical and ongoing endeavor.

An immense number of naive CD4+ T cell clones survey the secondary lymphoid organs. T cell receptor (TCR) sequencing approaches have estimated that the naive repertoire of a mouse consists of 2 × 106 clones, each expressing a unique TCR (1). Although such a diverse repertoire is necessary to recognize and protect against the vast array of pathogens an organism may encounter, it also presents the immune system with a challenge: Very small populations of cells must expand, functionally differentiate, and disperse throughout the body to effectively clear a pathogen. Remarkably, these processes occur simultaneously in a tightly regulated series of transcriptional programs that we are only starting to understand.

CD4+ T cell activation is initiated when a TCR recognizes a specific peptide presented on class II major histocompatibility complexes (MHC-II) expressed by antigen-presenting cells (APCs) (2). Inputs integrated from TCR binding, signaling downstream of costimulatory molecules, and innate cell–derived cytokines are incorporated into transcriptional networks that direct the expansion, gain of effector function, and migration of a responding naive cell. For example, in a T helper type 1 (Th1) response, an epitope-specific cell population can expand from several hundred to several hundred thousand cells, gain the ability to express a variety of cytokines (e.g., IFN-γ, IL-2, TNF, and IL-10), and migrate to various tissues to activate downstream target cells. Our current understanding of the coordination of these various programs is the subject of this review.

Each naive CD4+ T cell clone has the potential to differentiate into one of several functionally distinct effector programs, generally referred to as a subset (3). This gives a rare epitope-specific CD4+ T cell the flexibility to provide a diverse array of tailored instructions to activate cells responding to a specific pathogen. This is critical, as an aberrant or inappropriate CD4+ T cell response can lead to a lapse in pathogen control or the development of pathology. In this review, we revisit the original Th1/Th2 paradigm that described these distinct functional programs and place it in the context of our current understanding of CD4+ T cell responses to infection and allergy in vivo. We additionally discuss how a CD4+ T cell integrates numerous cues from APCs to differentiate into either a functionally active effector cell or a long-lived memory cell.

The advent of advanced in vivo experimental systems, in conjunction with epigenetics and transcriptomics, has provided insights into CD4+ T cell responses that were not predicted by the original CD4+ T cell paradigms derived from reductionist systems. Herein we review the evidence for a model of CD4+ T cell differentiation that incorporates at least two levels of diversification: (a) subset diversification, which encompasses the program of inflammatory effector cytokines that a CD4+ T cell produces (e.g., Th1, Th2, Th17) in response to signals predominately provided by the innate cell cytokine milieu, and (b) activation state diversification, which comprises the influence of signals downstream of the TCR that direct whether an individual CD4+ T cell clone becomes a high-cytokine-producing T effector (Teff) cell or a B cell–helping T follicular helper (Tfh) cell ( Figure 1 ). The Teff and Tfh states create bifurcated but parallel axes that work in concert to clear pathogens. For example, in a Th2 response, CD4+ Th2 Teff cells home to tissues and express the eosinophil-recruiting factor IL-5, while Th2 Tfh cells activate B cells to produce IgE and IgG1 antibodies that can activate granulocytes at the site of infection (4,5,6,7). We explain how these responses develop and discuss how interactions with various cell types both during and after priming influence an individual CD4+ T cell's fate.

sections.title: A BRIEF HISTORY OF THE DISCOVERY OF CD4+ T CELL SUBSETS

blocks.html: It has been known for many years that CD4+ T cells exhibit pleiotropic functions. While CD8+ T cells were known to be cytotoxic during lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus (LCMV) infection and graft rejection, CD4+ T cells were thought to assist in humoral responses, indirectly activate macrophages, and directly suppress inflammation (8,9,10,11). Additional CD4+ functional heterogeneity was recognized in 1981, when patients with acquired immunodeficiency presented with both an absence of circulating CD4+ T cells and a myriad of opportunistic infections (12,13,14). Understanding the function and generation of distinct populations of CD4+ T cells that could control a given bacterial, fungal, parasitic, or viral infection became of paramount importance.

Seminal work by Coffman, Mosmann, and colleagues initiated a period of discovery defining the factors associated with CD4+ T cell functional heterogeneity (15). Importantly, they demonstrated that individual clonal lines of differentiated CD4+ T cells could express different lymphokine profiles. Different lymphokine phenotypes induced mutually exclusive functional programs in target cells. This connection between CD4+ T cell subset cytokine production and resulting effector function was an exciting conceptual advance and raised the possibility of additional heterogeneity. These studies and others suggested that “the full range of Th cell phenotypes may be broader” than first realized, inspiring many investigations into the functional possibilities of CD4+ T cells (15, p. 2355; 16). By the early 2000s, the transcription factors that imparted specific effector cytokine profiles in Th1, Th2, and Th17 subsets had been elucidated. Zheng & Flavell (17) identified GATA3 in Th2 cells, Szabo, Glimcher, and colleagues hunted down T-bet in Th1 cells (18, 19), and Ivanov, Littman, and colleagues identified RORγt as the key transcription factor in Th17 cells (20).

A model for CD4+ T cell differentiation rapidly emerged in which cytokines from innate cells (induced by ligation of innate cell pattern recognition receptors) drove specific CD4+ effector subset programs. Lineage-enforcing transcription factors regulated CD4+ T cell cytokine secretion, coordinating a specific effector program that resulted in target cell activation. Many of the key findings supporting this model and the transcriptional and epigenetic regulation of CD4+ subsets have been discussed in recent reviews and are only briefly touched upon here (3, 21,22,23). Instead, we present an updated model of CD4+ effector T cell differentiation and a holistic view of CD4+ T cell responses in vivo. We incorporate recent work defining the cues that regulate how Teff and Tfh cells differentiate from naive precursors, as well as how both populations retain hallmarks of the inflammatory environment in which they were primed and propagate these responses in specific locations throughout the body.

sections.title: MOVING THE CD4+ T CELL FIELD IN VIVO

blocks.html: Early studies attempting to unravel the cues that influence CD4+ T cell fate necessitated the use of reductionist in vitro approaches, yet there were obvious limitations. Altering individual culture conditions, including the amount of TCR stimulation, the class of pathogen recognition receptor ligand, or the cocktail of cytokines in the medium, elucidated key factors that could alter T cell fate (reviewed in 23). Whether or not similar cues were perceived by CD4+ T cells in the complex microenvironment of the lymph node, however, was unclear. In addition, key aspects of time and location were taken out of the equation, making it difficult to apply this information to more translational applications.

The advent of genetically manipulated mice and development of techniques to visualize antigen-specific T cell responses revolutionized our understanding of CD4+ T cell differentiation in vivo (24). The adoptive transfer of naive TCR transgenic cells expressing distinct congenic markers into unimmunized mice allowed for the identification and visualization of a nascent, developing T cell response. Transferred congenic populations could be assayed directly ex vivo after immunization or infection using immunofluorescent histology, flow cytometry, or multiphoton confocal microscopy (25). These techniques provided a first glimpse into the kinetics of the CD4+ T cell response through time and space, including the visualization of the APCs involved in priming the CD4+ T cell response and the first description of the migration of CD4+ memory cells throughout the body (26, 27). The development of cytokine reporter mice permitted direct ex vivo assessment of function without additional manipulation (28), while mice generated to express photoactivatable fluorophores allowed for analysis of migration (29). Although the murine immune system will never fully replicate that of a human, and there exist potential caveats to using mice from genetically disparate backgrounds, most immunological principles have been defined using these tractable genetic models (30).

Soon after the advent of adoptive transfer, several labs demonstrated that the number of monoclonal TCR transgenic T cells transferred into a host prior to immunization could alter the ensuing response (as measured by proliferative burst, memory longevity, and function) due to T cell competition for peptide:MHC (pMHC) (31,32,33). These findings had two very important effects on the field: The first was to highlight the major role that the degree of interactions between the TCR and pMHC played in deciding a T cell's fate. The second was to increase the urgency to generate tools to study the endogenous CD4+ T cell response with normal naive precursor frequencies of anywhere between 1 and 600 cells (34,35,36). Shortly thereafter, MHC-II tetramers and techniques to study rare populations of epitope-specific CD4+ T cells in both humans and mice were developed (37). Below, we focus on the principles that these relatively recent advances have revealed and present a current model of the endogenous, antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response in vivo.

sections.title: THE T FOLLICULAR HELPER CELL CONUNDRUM

blocks.html: The discovery of a distinct population of B cell–helping Tfh cells added complexity to the CD4+ T cell field. The dogma of the linear connection between APCs, CD4+ effector subsets, and downstream effector programs was thrown into disarray. Although it was known for many years that CD4+ T cells were critical for T-dependent B cell responses and germinal center (GC) responses, the identity of the helping cells in vivo was unclear, yet often associated with Th2 responses (38, 39). Particularly perplexing was the observation that different types of antibody-secreting cells were generated in response to pathogens associated with different CD4+ effector T cell subsets (15). Seminal work on the chemokine receptor CXCR5 (previously known as BLR1) distinguished follicle-homing Tfh cells from other CD4+ T cell subsets and allowed for their subsequent identification and interrogation in vivo (40). Activated “B follicular helper” CD4+ T cells upregulate expression of CXCR5, migrate toward CXCL13-expressing B cell follicles, and provide help to B cells to undergo class-switch recombination and somatic hypermutation in mice and humans (41,42,43,44,45).

For several years, Tfh cells were characterized as a nonpolarized B cell–helping population that was distinct from previously described Teff subsets (46). This characterization was supported by early studies indicating that Tfh cells express high amounts of transcript for the transcriptional repressor BCL6, which, among many other functions, could inhibit Th1 and Th2 programs (47). In a pivotal study by Goodnow, Vinuesa, and colleagues, a genetic screen for autoimmune regulators revealed an enhanced Tfh population in the sanroque mouse due to aberrant regulation of ICOS (48). This allowed for a more detailed transcriptional analysis that identified a unique transcriptome for Tfh cells, further differentiating them from Th1 and Th2 cells (48). BCL6 was subsequently defined as the master transcription factor of Tfh cells and shown to be critical for supporting Tfh formation and function (49,50,51). BCL6 was also discovered to have an antagonistic relationship with the transcriptional activator Blimp-1, which is important for the terminal differentiation of high-cytokine-producing effector CD4+ T cells, again further distinguishing this population from effector-cytokine-producing CD4+ T cells (49, 52).

Many recent reviews have focused on the discovery and function of Tfh cells (53, 54). We alternatively review the evidence supporting the model that Tfh cells are not a distinct lineage but instead represent an activation state within any given effector subset (see the sidebar titled A Quick Word About the Nomenclature). By retaining hallmarks of the effector program that a naive CD4+ T cell encounters during priming, Tfh cells are endowed with the ability to drive different antibody isotype expression to help clear a pathogen and synergistically propagate an effector subset program.

sections.title: A QUICK WORD ABOUT THE NOMENCLATURE

blocks.html: As the field of CD4+ T cell biology has evolved, the nomenclature for various cellular states and subsets has also evolved. Subsets have been redefined based on newly discovered surface markers, cytokines, and transcription factors that various populations of CD4+ T cells express. Creating a meaningful nomenclature as we refine our understanding of CD4+ T cells is an important task of a review. While this was previously addressed (55), herein we refine the attributes associated with the currently accepted terminology.

T effector (Teff) cells are CXCR5−, Blimp-1high, and BCL6low cells that express the highest concentration of a lineage-defining transcription factor within an epitope-specific population and subsequently produce rapid and copious amounts of effector cytokines when restimulated (49). Teff cells can reside in the red pulp or periarteriolar lymphoid sheaths (PALS) of the spleen or in the paracortex of the lymph node as well as in nonlymphoid tissue following infection or antigen exposure (27, 103, 132, 133). In a Th1 infection, these cells are precursors to effector memory T (Tem) cells.

T follicular helper (Tfh) cells express intermediate levels of fate-associated factors within an epitope-specific population including CXCR5, BCL6, and effector subset transcription factors (e.g., T-bet), and they can express effector cytokines when restimulated. Recent evidence suggests Tfh cells are also an early source of IL-2 and express IL-21 (47, 49,50,51, 68, 69, 83, 134,135,136). They reside on both sides of the T-B border (65). Our previous studies referred to these cells as central memory T (Tcm) precursors, as they can form Tcm cells in response to an attenuated bacterial infection.

Germinal center (GC) Tfh cells are distinguished from Tfh cells by increased expression of proteins associated with Tfh identity (CXCR5, BCL6, ICOS, PD1, IL-4) and lower expression of genes associated with the Teff program (T-bet, Blimp-1) (61, 65, 66). GC Tfh cells reside in the GC (68, 137).

We provide evidence that Teff, Tfh, and GC Tfh populations can develop within various CD4+ helper subset programs (Th1, Th2, Th17). We therefore support the model proposed by Cannons, Lu, and Schwartzberg (138) in which the effector subset identifier is added to the population name. For example, in a Th1 inflammatory environment, populations would be referred to as Teff1, Tfh1, and GC Tfh1, while in a Th2 inflammatory environment they would be referred to as Teff2, Tfh2, and GC Tfh2 (see Figure 2 ).

sections.title: IN VIVO DIFFERENTIATION OF ANTIGEN-SPECIFIC CD4+ T CELLS
Teff and Tfh Are Activation States Within an Effector Program

blocks.html: The characterization of Tfh cells as a distinct lineage dominated the field for some time (55). Tfh cells displayed many of the attributes used to define other CD4+ effector subsets: They expressed a master transcription factor (BCL6) (46, 50), could be differentiated in vitro with exposure to cytokines (IL-6 and IL-21 via STAT3 signaling) (46, 56), and suppressed the expression of transcription factors and cytokines associated with alternative cell fates (49,50,51). However, in vivo experimentation began to erode this characterization, as further studies suggested that perhaps something other than the traditional, linear determination of effector subsets via master transcription factors and specific cytokine programs could be happening. Tfh cells were shown to form in the absence of STAT3, and neither IL-6 nor IL-21 was sufficient to drive Tfh differentiation in vivo (57, 58). It was also noted by several groups that BCL6 is expressed by most activated T cells shortly after TCR stimulation (59,60,61). IL-4 expression, previously associated with Th2 effector function, was found to be produced in the lymphoid organs by Tfh cells that also expressed BCL6 in both Th1 and Th2 inflammatory conditions (see the sidebar titled IL-4 Is Produced by Tfh Cells in Spleens and Lymph Nodes). Finally, the examination of circulating Tfh cells in human blood demonstrated the presence of low levels of effector subset transcription factors including T-bet, GATA3, and RORγt (62). Consequently, understanding how Tfh cells differentiated and functioned in vivo and whether or not the molecular pathways governing these programs were related to previously described Th cell effector subset programs became an important focus of study for the field.

sections.title: IL-4 IS PRODUCED BY Tfh CELLS IN SPLEENS AND LYMPH NODES

blocks.html: Although it is still possible to find textbooks and websites that cite T helper type 2 (Th2) production of IL-4 in the secondary lymphoid organs as the primary regulator of B cell class-switching, this is inaccurate. This confusion is created by the fact that both Th2 cells and T follicular helper (Tfh) cells are capable of producing IL-4. There is much evidence demonstrating that although IL-4 can be produced by both Th2 and Tfh cells in vivo, the location, regulation, and downstream effects of IL-4 production are distinct between these two populations.

Early evidence that Th2 cells were not the key B cell–helping population came from experiments in mice that lacked key molecules required for Th2 differentiation. Surprisingly, the ablation of either STAT6 or IL-4 protein (critical for Th2 development in vitro) resulted in no loss of germinal center (GC) B cells or Tfh development in vivo (139). An important series of experiments using IL-4 reporter mice further challenged the in vitro paradigms. The generation of a bicistronic IL-4 reporter in which GFP was inserted into the 3′UTR (4-get) uncoupled the expression of IL-4 transcript from the production of IL-4 protein (140). As other IL-4 reporter mice generated with insertions into the IL-4 locus accurately reflect IL-4 protein production (141,142,143), Mohrs and colleagues generated dual reporter mice that separately express reporters for both IL-4 transcript and protein production called 4get-KN2 mice (144). In 2009, several groups used these 4get-KN2 mice to define the subsets of cells that produce IL-4 in the lymph node and lung during a Th2 response. 4get-KN2 mice were injected with Th2-inducing stimuli including N. brasiliensis (145), Heligmosomoides polygyrus (146), and schistosome egg extract (147). IL-4-protein-producing cells in the lymph node also expressed the Tfh-associated markers CXCR5, ICOS, and BCL6 in both type 1 and type 2 inflammatory conditions. These cells could also produce IL-21 and were found at the T-B border, within the B cell follicles and GCs (145,146,147 and data not shown). Remarkably, IL-4-competent transcript-expressing cells found throughout the T cell area did not express IL-4 protein unless further activated through additional stimulation (145). IL-4-producing Tfh cells in the lymph node were shown to be phenotypically and functionally distinct from GATA3+ IL-4-producing Th2 cells in the lung, which could also promote eosinophilia in transfer experiments (145). Later studies demonstrated that even the regulation of IL-4 expression is different in Tfh and Th2 cells. Specifically, a 3′ enhancer in the IL-4 locus (called HSV or CNS-2) that was found to be critical for IL-4 production by Tfh cells in the lymph node did not affect Th2 responses in the tissue (148, 149). Therefore, in response to infection or immunization in vivo, IL-4 production in the lymph node is a hallmark feature of Tfh cells, and cytokine-producing, differentiated Th2 effector cells are found in the nonlymphoid tissue. Analyzing transcription factor expression (levels of GATA3 and BCL6) and direct ex vivo cytokine production may better distinguish these cell types.

There was a period of intense focus on both human (62, 63) and murine Tfh cell function and differentiation and how these cells fit into the context of a developing CD4+ T cell response. Three separate studies were published in 2011 that interrogated the factors regulating the progression of an antigen-specific CD4+ T cell response in vivo. Crotty and colleagues (64) focused on the early cues regulating Tfh differentiation. Jenkins and colleagues (65) focused on the development and function of CXCR5+ central memory cells and their effector cell precursors, while Kaech and colleagues (66) interrogated whether rules governing CD8+ T cell memory formation applied to CD4+ memory T cell differentiation. Although different infections, model systems, population-defining surface markers, and nomenclature were used in the three studies, the concepts that emerged were remarkably consistent and defined the framework for our model.

The model we present is characterized by an early bifurcation of Teff and Tfh cells within the same effector program. Within three days of infection, an epitope-specific population undergoes an early bifurcation into CD25<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> T-bet<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">high</sup> Blimp-1<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> Teff cells or CXCR5<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> BCL6-expressing Tfh cells. Both B cells and ICOS are involved in the instruction of the Tfh population, although different conclusions were drawn about when these signals were required. IL-2 signaling via IL-2Rα expression is required for the generation of CXCR5<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">−</sup> Teff cells, and this is associated with the maintenance of high expression of T-bet in a Th1 response. These studies also provided evidence that the development of the CD4<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> T cell response is dynamic: The migration of CD4<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> T cells—and accordingly, the cells with which they interact—influences their differentiation.

These studies and others revealed gradients of expression of transcription factors, surface markers, and secreted molecules that define a CD4+ T cell's ultimate fate. T-bethigh BCL6low effector cells and BCL6high T-betlow GC Tfh cells expressed opposing programs defined by multiple factors, while a population of CXCR5int PD1low Tfh (or pre-Tfh) cells that expressed an intermediate phenotype with characteristics of each population also existed. These findings suggest that despite an early bifurcation between Teff and Tfh cells, the gradient of expression of factors that regulate differentiation can change over time and be either altered or enforced by subsequent cellular interactions. For example, early Tfh cells express intermediate levels of CXCR5, which allows them to migrate to the T-B border, and only upon additional interactions with B cells do they further upregulate CXCR5 and the transcriptional program associated with GC Tfh cells (55, 67). Importantly, this helps to explain how CXCR5int Tfh cells can exhibit characteristics of both Th1 cells and GC Tfh cells as they express intermediate levels of both BCL6 and T-bet (5, 61, 65, 66, 68,69,70,71). Intermediate levels of BCL6 and effector program transcription factors may be important for cytokine production at the T-B border, as class-switch recombination in a T-dependent B cell predominantly occurs prior to the formation of the GC, implicating Tfh and not GC Tfh cells as the major drivers of this process (72, 73).

We are only now starting to understand how these various transcriptional networks interact and influence each other. For example, work by Weinmann and colleagues demonstrated that T-bet and BCL6 can physically interact, to generate a T-bet-BCL6 complex that can mask the DNA-binding domain of BCL6, creating direct competition between these two transcription factors (74). Although there is still much work to be done to elucidate how these programs are regulated in different inflammatory environments, it is clear that similar bifurcations of Teff and Tfh cells also occur in vivo in epitope-specific populations in the context of Th2 and Th17 inflammation (75, 76). Most recently, a Tfh13 population that is different from Tfh2 cells was shown to emerge in the lymph node after exposure to Alternaria and drive high-affinity IgE production, but it is unclear how these cells relate to previously described populations (77).

sections.title: INTERACTIONS BETWEEN TCR AND pMHC-II INFLUENCE THE Teff VERSUS Tfh DECISION

blocks.html: For 50 years, the strength of TCR stimulation has been implicated in influencing CD4+ T cell fate (56, 78,79,80,81). The very early bifurcation of Teff and Tfh cells within an epitope-specific population again focused attention on the role of TCR signaling in the CD4+ T cell fate decision. Newly developed tools and techniques made it feasible to study both monoclonal TCR transgenic and polyclonal tetramer-specific populations responding to the same epitope. In addition, TCR transgenic animals generated with TCRs of varying affinities for the same epitope could be used to determine the influence of TCR signal strength on the Teff and Tfh decision. Tubo, Jenkins, and colleagues (82) took the Herculean approach of transferring individual naive T cells via in vivo limiting dilution assays to determine whether naive cells with different TCRs underwent different patterns of development in response to Listeria infection. This system revealed that each naive T cell has a tendency to produce certain patterns of Teff versus Tfh cells, although the composite of all various clones resembled the approximate 50/50 split between Teff and Tfh populations seen in a given polyclonal, endogenous epitope-specific population (82). TCR signaling can be varied by TCR affinity, the amount of pMHC-II perceived by a given TCR, or the length of time a given TCR cell spends proofreading APC-presented pMHC-II (referred to as dwell time). Modeling of the results suggested that cells with a short dwell time are fated to become Tfh cells and those with a longer dwell time become Teff cells, while those with the longest dwell time become GC Tfh cells (82). This is in agreement with a more recent study also using Listeria infection that demonstrated that naive cells that receive the strongest TCR signals produce IL-2 and are fated to become Tfh cells (83).

In opposition to this data, however, several other studies addressing a similar question have agreed that Teff cells are induced by strong TCR stimulation and Tfh cells derive from lower-affinity interactions. For example, King and colleagues demonstrated that T cells activated by increasing affinities underwent more expansion and increased Th1 differentiation, while those activated by low-affinity antigen differentiated into Tfh cells and depended upon B cells for additional differentiation (84). These findings were supported by studies in a viral system that also showed that high TCR affinity was associated with preferential Teff cell differentiation (85). So while the relationship between TCR affinity and the decision to become a Teff or Tfh cell is clearly influenced by TCR affinity, some controversy still remains, especially regarding the GC Tfh cells. One possibility is that the GC Tfh cell, which is thought to be primed by dendritic cells (DCs) but can then undergo additional TCR stimulation from antigen-presenting B cells, may not be regulated by the same rules. GC Tfh differentiation may instead depend more upon antigen persistence, allowing for cumulative TCR signaling events (86). The entanglement of Tfh cells by varying levels of ICOSL on B cells through ICOS-ICOSL interactions may also de-emphasize the effect of TCR:pMHC-II dwell time on GC Tfh cell fate (87).

And while there is still much work to be done investigating these fate decisions, some of the molecular mechanisms connecting TCR affinity and the Teff and Tfh bifurcation have been elucidated. Krishnamoorthy et al. (88) demonstrated that IRF4, previously determined to be involved in both CD8+ T cell and B cell fate decisions downstream of their antigen receptors, also governs the CD4+ Teff-Tfh axis. Higher levels of TCR signaling translated into higher IRF4 levels and subsequently shifted the BCL6-Blimp-1 balance toward a Teff fate. Forced expression of IRF4 was sufficient to promote Teff differentiation independent of IL-2 receptor signaling. Conversely, genetic ablation of IRF4 severely impacted Th1 cytokine expression and lowered expression of glucose transporters and enzymes involved in glycolysis (89). This defect in anabolic metabolism in IRF4-deficient CD4+ T cells is associated with a lack of PI3K/mTOR activation (90). Taken together, these findings indicate that the TCR signal strength, controlled by TCR affinity for a given pMHC-II as well as antigen load, can instruct the functional outcome of a CD4+ T cell by modulating IRF4 levels that regulate BCL6 and Blimp-1 levels and metabolic pathways that are important in fate differentiation. In addition, TCR affinity has been implicated in altering the expression of CD25, with higher-affinity TCR interactions leading to heightened expression of CD25 and a greater proportion of Teff cells (91). It will be important to dissect how signaling pathways downstream of the TCR intersect with additional signals from cytokine and costimulatory receptor molecules to define a specific CD4+ T cell fate.

sections.title: INTERACTIONS WITH ANTIGEN-PRESENTING CELLS THAT BIAS CD4+ T CELL ACTIVATION STATE

blocks.html: In addition to TCR signal strength, the identity of the APC that activates a CD4+ T cell can also influence its differentiation and functional outcome. There is a vast array of APCs that can be involved in T cell priming (92,93,94). While the role of APCs influencing CD4+ T cell fate has largely focused on the T effector program, there is evidence that various APCs can influence the Teff versus Tfh decision as well. After antigen administration, Tfh-promoting DCIR2+ CD4+ DCs that express ICOSL and localize to the outer T cell zone interact with CD4+ T cells expressing the G protein–coupled receptor EB12 (GPR183) to promote a Tfh cell fate in a B cell–independent manner (95). These DCs also produce soluble and membrane-bound forms of CD25 to quench local IL-2 to further reinforce Tfh differentiation. Migratory DCs can also prime Tfh cells, as CD11b+ conventional type 2 DCs (cDC2s) were found to express homing molecules that position them at the T-B border upon entry into the lymph node following intranasal OVA+LPS administration (96). Mice that are deficient in cDC2s have a reduction in protective antibody generation following infection with inactivated influenza A PR8, demonstrating their importance in Tfh differentiation (96). Interestingly, B cells have recently been described to also possess the potential to activate naive CD4+ T cells and drive Tfh formation in response to virus-like particle administration and Plasmodium infection (97, 98). It is clear that differences in APC expression of costimulatory receptors, soluble factors, or the amount of pMHC-II presented also influence CD4+ Teff versus Tfh fate decisions, and this is an active area of research.

sections.title: Th1 AND Th2 FUNCTION IN VIVO

blocks.html: While much of this review has focused on the early decisions of Tfh and Teff cell subsets, recent technological advances have also enhanced our understanding of how different CD4+ effector subsets migrate out of the lymphoid organs to the tissues and function once there (99,100,101). Work from many labs has defined the expression of unique chemokine receptors within individual effector subset programs in both humans and mice (e.g., CXCR3 on Th1 cells, CRTh2 on Th2 cells, and CCR6 on Th17 cells) (102). Additionally, the terminal differentiation of a T cell is influenced by the tissue in which it resides. Various cell types located in distinct compartments of lymphoid tissue or in the peripheral tissue itself can continue to impact cellular fate ( Figure 2 ). We therefore focus on recent knowledge of the migration, differentiation, and function of CD4+ T cells in tissues.

CD4+ Teff cells control pathogens by migrating into tissues and secreting cytokines that recruit and activate innate cells. Cytokine production by CD4+ effector cells is controlled by both the presence of antigen and the presentation of peptide on MHC-II. A study by McLachlan et al. (103) used direct ex vivo staining for IFN-γ in the absence of restimulation to demonstrate that little to no IFN-γ is produced in the lymph nodes during an acute response. Yet at the same time points after immunization, T effector cells making IFN-γ (Teff1) were doing so at the site of antigen injection (103). This local cytokine production can be inhibited by injection of antibodies against MHC-II, demonstrating the requirement for ongoing recognition of pMHC-II by CD4+ Teff1 cells to make cytokine (103). The restriction of cytokine production by CD4+ Th1 cells that recognize presented antigen on APCs was further delineated using intravital imaging in the skin. Honda et al. (104) found that during local antigen exposure, effector CD4+ T cells interact with APCs, cease migration in a transient fashion, produce a burst of cytokine, and then continue to migrate. Continued migration is dependent on PD-1/PD-L1 interaction, as blockage of PD-L1 on APCs leads to longer dwell time of the CD4+ T cells and greater amounts of cytokine production (104). The dependence of cytokine production on interactions with APCs and TCR signaling was further demonstrated in infection models utilizing either Mycobacterium tuberculosis or influenza A virus (105). Cytokine production by CD4+ T cells in the lung is restricted to areas of high antigen abundance, and influenza A infection generates more cytokine in the lung due to higher antigen load (105). Thus, local antigen presence and presentation by APCs in nonlymphoid tissue control the production and levels of Th1 cytokine secreted by CD4+ Teff1 cells.

Effector CD4+ T cells that secrete type 2 cytokines (Teff2 cells) are primed in the lymphoid organs and terminally differentiate in the tissues. Identifying the APCs that prime the Th2 response has been an area of active research for many years. CD301b+ DCs in the skin were shown to transport antigen and drive Th2 polarization in the lymph node in response to subcutaneous ovalbumin (OVA) admixed with papain or alum (106). In mice depleted of their CD301b+ dermal DCs, there was a decrease in GATA-3+ CD4+ cell division and IgE production in response to Nippostrongylus brasiliensis infection, further demonstrating the importance of this subset of DCs on Th2 differentiation (106). It was recently recognized that CD301b+ DC entry into the parenchymal regions of the lymph node is mediated through CCR8 (107). In response to an allergen, CCL8, the ligand for CCR8, was found to be produced by CD169+ SIGN-R1+ macrophages in the lymph node. Production of CCL8 orchestrated migration and concomitant activation of a distinct subset of DCs expressing CCR8 and CD301b to a region of the lymph node where they facilitate priming of Teff2 cells (107). In CCR8-deficient mice, CD301b+ DCs were unable to migrate from subcapsular sinuses into parenchymal compartments of lymph nodes, resulting in abrogated Teff2 responses (107). These CD301b+ dermal DCs also play important roles outside of the lymph node, as intravital imaging has shown that these cells can relay allergens from the blood to IgE-bound mast cells in the perivascular space, stimulating their degranulation (108). Thus, specialized subsets of APCs can prime CD4+ T cells and promote their differentiation toward a Teff2 cell fate and assist innate effectors in Th2 responses.

Once a Teff2 cell is primed in the secondary lymphoid organs, it can migrate to nonlymphoid tissues, where its function is regulated through tissue-restricted mechanisms. Of interest, these Teff2 cells that become terminally differentiated after incorporating cues from nonlymphoid tissues become more innate-like and share many features with type 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2s). Specifically, in the absence of epithelial-derived cytokine receptor signaling (TSLP, IL25, and IL33), Teff2 cells in the lung fail to express IL-5 and IL-13 and exhibit full effector function (109). IL-33R expression has also been associated with subsets of memory Th2 cells that exhibit increased pathogenicity both in mice and in humans. Specifically, Endo et al. (110) demonstrated that pathogenic Th2 cells coexpress GATA-3 and ST2 in nonlymphoid tissue. Signaling through p38-MAP kinase downstream of the IL-33R was shown to directly induce IL-5 production by memory Th2 cells in mice and humans (110). A similar subset has been found in mice, as a unique phenotypic subset of circulating Th2 cells termed Th2A is associated with atopic allergic disease in human blood (111). Unlike conventional Th2 cells, Th2A cells express CRTh2 as well as high levels of IL1RL1 transcript, a component of the IL-33R (111). The signaling in nonlymphoid tissues that controls Th2 function and the ubiquity of these signals in various organs, infections, and diseases continue to be a focus in the field.

A recent focus in type 2 immunity has been the intersection between cytokine-producing Teff2 cells and nonimmune cells. IL-13 production by Teff2 cells has been shown to be essential for airway hyperresponsiveness (AHR) development in a neonatal model of allergic airway inflammation, making it an obvious therapeutic target (112). After allergen challenge, neonatal mice lacking CD4+ T cell production of IL-13 were protected from developing AHR even though eosinophilia, IL-33, and ILC2 numbers were elevated in the lung (112). Interestingly, Teff2 cells can also secrete IL-13 and amphiregulin in an antigen-independent manner in response to IL-33. This antigen-independent production of Th2 cytokines enhances fibrosis (as well as pathogenic effects of eosinophils) (113, 114). IL-13 and IL-4 production can also cause chronic itch, which was ameliorated in a model of atopic dermatitis in mice that do not express IL-4Ra on neurons (115). Therefore the Teff2-expressed cytokine IL-13 can act directly on numerous cell types including neurons, nonhematopoietic cells, and immune cells to promote symptoms of type 2 diseases.

Another recent focus in type 2 immunity is the tissue localization that allows for the interactions of these various cell types. Work by Molofsky and colleagues (116) has highlighted the importance of the adventitial cuff of the lung as one of these sites. Located proximal to the bronchi and large vessels, it contains adventitial stromal cells (ASCs), a mesenchymal cell type that produces IL-33 and TSLP (116). ILC2s, Teff2 cells, and even naive CD4+ T cells can migrate to adventitial cuffs via the lung parenchyma or through egress from the high endothelial venules (HEVs) contained within these sites (116). Depletion of ASCs causes disruption of adventitial cuff formation and leads to a loss of both ILC2s and Teff2 accumulation upon helminth infection (116). These adventitial cuffs and other structures in nonlymphoid tissue, such as inducible bronchus-associated lymphoid tissue (iBALT) (discussed below), contribute to the recruitment and maintenance of Teff2 cells and other CD4+ subsets and are an area of continued research as we strive to learn how these cells interact in vivo.

The formation and persistence of functional CD4+ memory T cells following pathogen clearance are critical in generating long-lasting effective immunity that protects against reinfection. After the expansion of a naive CD4+ T cell clone following activation, 90% of the cells die by apoptosis in a stage referred to as contraction (117). At least three distinct subsets of memory CD4+ T cells have been described: CCR7+ central memory T (Tcm) cells, CCR7− effector memory T (Tem) cells, and tissue-resident memory T (Trm) cells (118). Delineating precursor relationships for these various populations continues to be a major focus of the CD4+ field. Unlike CD8+ T cells, which change phenotype between the effector stage and the memory stage, CD4+ memory populations appear to reflect and emerge from their differentiated effector populations (119). This was originally described by Harrrington et al. using IFN-γ reporter mice to show that memory CD4+ T cells can arise from IFN-γ-competent effector CD4+ T cells (120). This suggested that at least in Th1 infections, some memory CD4+ T cells did not arise from a distinct developmental pathway, but instead were a product of the effector pool. Subsequent studies using various genetically ablated mice and mixed bone marrow chimeras demonstrated that Tcm cell formation was dependent on BCL6 and ICOS:ICOSL interactions, and that these cells expressed CCR7 and CXCR5, resembling Tfh cells. Transfer of Tfh cells 10 days after infection, when they already expressed CCR7, into naive mice demonstrated that these cells persisted and retained a Tcm phenotype (65). Furthermore, the development of Teff1 and Tem cells, but not Tcm cells, depended upon CD25. Recent work by Ciucci et al. (121) confirmed these results and demonstrated by single-cell RNA-seq that formation of CD4+ Tcm cells is dependent on the transcription factor Thpok. Expression of Thpok suppresses the expression of transcription factors associated with effector function (Blimp-1 and Runx3) and allows for the formation of a functional memory CD4+ T cell compartment. It is unclear whether the Tfh precursor/Tcm relationship will hold true under different inflammatory conditions. For example, in a Th2 response, CCR7+ cells can be found in both the CXCR5− and CXCR5+ populations at both early and late time points (75).

The formation and maintenance of memory CD4+ T cells are essential for protection against reinfection. Trm cells reside in nonlymphoid tissue and do not recirculate unless reactivated, serving as sentinels at the site of antigen exposure. Upon reinfection, these Trm cells survey the nonlymphoid tissues and can rapidly secrete cytokines and effector molecules that provide protection (122,123,124,125). CD4+ Th1 and Th2 Trm cells require signaling through CD25 for their migration or survival in the lung (75, 126). CD25-deficient CD4+ T cells do not form Teff1 cells in the lymph node and spleen or Trm cells in the lung at the same frequencies as CD25-sufficient cells following LCMV infection (126). Additionally, B cell–deficient mice have increased Trm cells in the lung early after LCMV infection, but the maintenance and survival of these Trm cells are heavily impacted by the lack of B cells (126).

In the lung, inflammation or infection can lead to the formation of tertiary lymphoid structures called iBALT, which contain loosely organized B cell follicles, T cell zones, and HEVs (127). Both CD4+ Trm cells and naive CD4+ T cells can localize to iBALT, either through HEVs contained within iBALT structures or from the lung parenchyma itself (128). Stromal cells within iBALT can secrete IL-7, which promotes survival of Th2 memory cells (129, 130). The factors that control the maintenance of CD4+ Trms appear to be tissue specific, as Iijima & Iwasaki (131) found that in HSV infection in the female reproductive tract, macrophages secrete CCL5, which is essential for the maintenance of CD4+ Trm cells. In the lung, infection with LCMV leads to CD4+ Trm cell formation that requires B cells for maintenance (126). Thus, the maintenance and survival of CD4+ T cells in nonlymphoid tissue are dependent on various cell types and are still an ongoing area of research.

Herein we have presented our current understanding of CD4<sup xmlns:f="http://www.example.org/functions">+</sup> T cell differentiation and function in vivo. There is still much work to do to understand how these cells promote resistance to infection and how best to induce different populations via vaccination.

figures.label: Figure 1
figures.captionHtml: A holistic model of CD4+ T cell differentiation in vivo. Our model of CD4+ T cell differentiation incorporates several layers of fate decisions over time and space. (Left) Phase 1 (priming): CD4+ T cells are primed on antigen-presenting cells. TCR signal strength impacts fate decisions. High TCR stimulation is associated with high expression of the IL-2 receptor alpha chain (CD25) and the transcription factors IRF4 and Blimp-1, but not the transcription factor BCL6. Low TCR stimulation is associated with low CD25 expression and IRF4 expression but higher BCL6 expression is associated with the upregulation of CXCR5 and migration to the T-B border as a T follicular helper (Tfh) cell. Concurrently, signals through cytokine receptors lead to the expression of the transcriptional networks that control a specific effector program (e.g., Th1, Th2, Th17). Interactions and competition between the TCR-induced transcriptional programs and the cytokine-induced transcriptional networks influence a cell's ultimate fate. In the example depicted, a naive clone that receives a strong TCR stimulation in the presence of IFN-γ and IL-12 will become a Th1 Teff cell (Teff1) that will express high levels of T-bet, STAT5, and Blimp-1 and can rapidly make IFN-γ upon TCR stimulation to help control acute infection. In this same priming environment, a clone that undergoes lower TCR signaling will express CXCR5 and migrate to the T-B border as an IFN-γ-secreting Tfh (Tfh1) cell. (Right) For simplicity's sake, we have shown the differentiation of Teff and Tfh cells during a Th1 inflammatory response, but this has also been shown to occur in a Th2 or Th17 response, as explained in the text. Phase 2 (reinforcement/terminal differentiation): Teff cells migrate to different tissues depending on the chemokine receptors they express. Teff1 cells can migrate into the red pulp, blood, and tissues, where they interact with their innate cells to release cytokines. Tfh1 cells migrate to the T-B border, where they interact with B cells. Interactions with B cells through receptor-ligand pairs (e.g., ICOS-ICOSL) and exchange of cytokines maintain the Tfh phenotype. Expression of effector subset–associated transcription factors allows a Tfh cell to express cytokines at the T-B border, including cytokines associated with the effector program (IFN-γ) and their Tfh state (e.g., IL-21). Productive T-B interactions allow Tfh cells to enter a GC, further upregulate BCL6, further downregulate T-bet, and drive B cell affinity maturation. Abbreviations: DC, dendritic cell; GC, germinal center; TCR, T cell receptor; Teff, T effector; Tfh, T follicular helper. Figure adapted from images created with BioRender.com.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.captionHtml: Distinct spatial and temporal roles for CD4+ T cells in response to infection or insult. The early bifurcation of Teff and Tfh cells leads to the development of differentiated Teff cells that home to the site of antigen exposure and secrete cytokines upon TCR stimulation. The cytokines that are secreted by CD4+ Teff cells can recruit and support innate effector cells, such as macrophages in Th1 responses and eosinophils and basophils in Th2-skewed environments. In contrast, CD4+ Tfh cells can interact with B cells at the T-B border and enter into the GC in secondary lymphoid organs, promoting class-switching and affinity maturation through secretion of cytokines such as IFN-γ by Tfh1 cells and IL-4 by Tfh2 cells. The antibodies produced by class-switched B cells can activate specific innate effectors that carry out functions tailored to Th1 or Th2 responses.
